title: Hierarchical memory and scalable architectures
transcript_provenance: Local machine transcription (faster-whisper small.en); not publisher captions
lecture_corrections: Dirty bit: the lecture says the dirty bit indicates non-coherency in multiprocessor systems. Drepper (2007, 3.2, p. 16) defines a dirty line as written and not yet written back, which occurs in a single-processor write-back cache. The chapter separates the write policy from coherence.

Memory speeds on the slide (SRAM '> 10 ns', DRAM '~ 40 ns') are device times. Pointer-chase measurements on this machine give 1.2 to 1.5 ns (L1), 3.7 to 4.4 ns (L2) and 123 to 162 ns (DRAM) as seen by a program (five runs, one 267 ns outlier excluded). Both are recorded with what each measures.

Cache block: the lecture's example block is a few words. The line of this machine is 64 bytes (16 words of 32 bits, 8 doubles), reported by sysfs and visible as the knee of the stride benchmark at a stride of 8 doubles; Drepper (p. 15) gives 32 bytes for early caches and 64 bytes as the norm.

Slide 'Processor 52% annually, Memory 7% annually' (credited to rankred.com): the rates are not in the sources opened (Hennessy and Patterson, Wulf and McKee were not opened). A constant 52 % for 30 years is 2.9e5, but the plotted processor curve ends near 2e4 (read by eye), so the label cannot describe the whole period.

NUMA example: the slide gives 'SGI's Altix ICE 8400 (> 64K cores)' as a NUMA machine. The core count is consistent with SGI's text (up to 65,536 compute nodes with multi-core processors, 1,536 cores per 128 processors), but SGI describes the ICE 8400 as a scale-out blade platform with quad data rate InfiniBand, which is a cluster of nodes with separate memories and is not NUMA (Drepper p. 43). SGI's shared-memory NUMA product of that generation was the Altix UV (single system image of up to 256 sockets and 16 TB, NUMAlink 5). Sources are vendor press text and a vendor slide deck, not datasheets.

Write-through: the lecture presents write-through with snooping as the way to avoid the coherency problem. This works but sends every store to the bus; most caches are write-back with a protocol such as MESI (Drepper 3.3.3, p. 25). The chapter quantifies the difference (coherence.py).
SMP limit 'typically 64 processors': no source opened states this number; recorded as a lecture claim.
source_uncertainties: Wulf and McKee (1995), 'Hitting the memory wall', ACM SIGARCH CAN 23(1) 20-24: the paper could not be opened (library copy returned an empty page behind a web firewall; the ACM page returned HTTP 403). Bibliographic data were checked in Crossref. The chapter cites the title only. Ertl's critique (opened) is cited for its description of the paper's argument; the paper's own growth rates were not read.

Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, was not opened. The AMAT formula and the three kinds of miss are cited to P. H. J. Kelly's Imperial College lecture notes (opened), which cite 6th edition appendix B.3, p. B22. The 52 %/7 % growth rates of the lecture slide are therefore unverified lecture claims.

Mattson, Gecsei, Slutz and Traiger (1970), IBM Systems Journal 9(2) 78-117, was not opened. The stack property is attributed to it through Kim, Hill and Wood (1991), whose extended abstract (opened) describes the stack and stack distance; Theorem 1 is proved in the chapter and checked by reuse.py.

SGI sources: the Altix ICE 8400 text is a press text reprinted on a web page that carries no date; the Altix UV material is an undated slide deck by an SGI employee that names the Nehalem-EX/Westmere-EX generation. Neither is a datasheet. The cores per ICE 8400 node were not stated; the lecture's '> 64K cores' agrees with the text by arithmetic (65,536 nodes with multi-core processors). That the ICE 8400 is a distributed-memory machine is the chapter's inference from 'scale-out blade platform' and InfiniBand, supported by Drepper p. 43.
The lecture's SMP limit of about 64 processors has no source among those opened. The chapter derives a bandwidth bound (p* = B_bus/g) and does not state a value.

Linux first-touch behaviour: the NUMA memory policy document (opened) states that the default policy is local allocation, an allocation on the node of the CPU where the allocation takes place. That a page is allocated when first touched (demand paging) is the author's statement and was not read in the document. Drepper (2007, 5.2, p. 44) describes striping as the 2007 default; the chapter prefers the current documentation and says so.

Intel ARK was read through a fetch agent on 2026-10-26 (8 cores, 4 P and 4 E, 12 threads, 12 MB Intel Smart Cache, at most 2 memory channels, four memory types, launched Q1 2022; no bandwidth figure). The installed memory type of the laptop was not determined, so no peak bandwidth is quoted.

Cache geometry (L1d 48 KiB 12-way, L2 1280 KiB 10-way, L3 12288 KiB 8-way, 64-byte lines) is what the WSL guest reports through sysfs for every logical processor; the guest's view is synthetic (6 cores x 2 threads reported for a 4P+4E processor). The simulators use these numbers. The L3 simulation uses modulo indexing; real L3 caches hash addresses over slices, so L3 results are directional. The physical address width was not determined; the tag-overhead example assumes 40 bits.

Timing measurements are noisy: hybrid core placement of the single thread, a virtual machine, and other jobs on the machine. Each timing listing prints the fifth of five runs; ranges quoted in the text are over those five runs. The sizes of effects are orders of magnitude, not precise values.

The pointer chase shows no L3 plateau (latency at 4 MiB is 107 to 126 ns, 0.8 to 1.0 times the DRAM latency at 16 MiB). The cause was not determined. Candidates: other jobs evicting L3 lines; address translation (in a virtual machine a TLB miss can need a walk of both the guest and the host page tables; no source for this was opened); a run on an efficient core, whose L2 is 2 MB shared by four cores (ServeTheHome; the E-core L1d size was not sourced) while the guest reports the performance-core geometry for every logical processor; or a higher L3 latency than assumed. A trial with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) (65,536 kB of huge pages reported for a 64 MiB region) changed latencies by at most 22 % at every size in two sessions; the host may still map the region with 4 KiB pages, so the trial does not exclude translation. The trial is not part of the listings.

The rise of the chase latency before the L2 capacity (4.5 to 4.8 ns at 512 KiB, 7.0 to 9.1 ns at 1 MiB) has three untested candidates: limited associativity with physical page placement, first-level data TLB misses, and runs on an efficient core. The rise of the stride benchmark above the knee (1.3 to 1.7 times from stride 8 to 16) was not isolated (page crossings and prefetchers are candidates).

Cachegrind (Valgrind 3.22) was run with --D1=49152,12,64 and a 16 MiB 16-way LL because it needs a power-of-two number of sets in the last level; only the D1 read misses of the two summing functions were compared, so no second simulator checked an L2 or L3 count. The L1d index bits lie inside the 4 KiB page offset, so the virtual-address model is exact for the L1d; the hardware L2 is physically indexed and the L3 hashed, so the simulator's L2 and L3 results are directional. The Valgrind manual was not opened. The simulators differ by at most 5 misses in 31,500 (0.016 %); the excess of one miss in most Cachegrind counts and the deficit of five at N = 500 were not traced.

The concurrencies of the overlap section (20.6 and 9.4 lines in flight) are implied averages that assume every miss waits 130 ns; the processor's limit on outstanding misses and the behaviour of its prefetchers are not described by any source opened.

Values alpha = 1.5 microseconds, 1/beta = 12.5 GB/s, NUMA factor rho = 1.5 and 2.5, mean time between failures of 5 years per node, and independent exponential failures are assumptions used for arithmetic. The speedups 61.3 and 1.23, the bisection times and the failure interval of 4.4 h are illustrations of the models, not data.

Topology: topology.py verifies bisection width, diameter and link count for 16 nodes only; formulas for other sizes are the standard ones and are not proved. Al-Fares et al. (2008) were read for the abstract, section 2.1 (oversubscription definition, p. 64) and section 3 (k^3/4 hosts, p. 66) only.
Exercise 6 reports three runs of a variant of rowcol.c (leading dimension) that is not in the repository; the numbers are those runs.

The implied concurrency of the column-order sum at N = 4096 (9.4 lines) assumes that every miss goes to DRAM; a hashing 12 MiB L3 may hold the 256 KiB of one column between passes, in which case L is the unmeasured L3 latency and the concurrency is lower.

review_rounds.notes: B1: the simulator is called exact for the L1d only (Cachegrind checked D1 only); L2 and L3 are directional (virtual indexing, physical L2, hashed L3) in #cache, #amat and #limits. B2: Exercise 5 charges a request and a reply in every option (300 ms for (i), about 3030 times (ii), 9.2 times for the dependent case). B3: L1 range 1.2 to 1.5 ns, ratio 6.5 to 8.4. M1: four candidate causes for the missing L3 plateau (jobs, two-level page walk, efficient core with 2 MB shared L2 per ServeTheHome, higher L3 latency); the huge-page trial does not exclude translation; the associativity explanation is stated as a candidate. M2: N = 4096 concurrency hedged for a hashed L3; Table 7.1 cell and wording changed. M3: core count agreed with the vendor text, only the NUMA label corrected; 'hybrid' mislabel replaced; Nehalem-EX generation named. M4: transcript wording removed from quotation marks; only slide text is quoted. M5: counter renamed 'transfers' in coherence.py; output refreshed. M6: sumcg.c added as a ninth exact listing before the Cachegrind session; the extra miss is stated as not traced. M7: banks n_b, stride sigma in stride.c prose, period q in Lemma 2; interleave.py header changed (kappa). m1: L3 mixture sentence reworded. m2: 'miss term'. m3: 'after the first pass'. m5: locality heading moved to 9:52 with 5:01 inline; NUMA picture link t = 1910. code_lab.py --chapter 7 rerun after the changes.
